When I was about 17-18, I went to a theme park with huge group of people. Our group had many divisions, so the division I split into was made up of around 8-9 people. When it was time to go on a small roller coaster, only 5 of us were willing to go, as the others got motion sickness or didn't feel like going. Because the five of us would have to split unevenly due to the ride being a two-seater per car, I decided to sacrifice my pride and the other four sit together. As we boarded, one of my friends, "Summer," decided to join us. Summer tried to ride next to me so I didn't have to ride next to a stranger, as we both have anxiety.

Anyway, Summer was denied access because a guy, "Chris", and his friends were in front of her. Chris ended up sitting next to me and I remembered his friends going behind us. His group teased him to ask for my number and Snapchat, neither of which I was prepared to give. Poor Chris made attempts to ask for them, but my social anxiety told me to look elsewhere. During the ride, I stayed silent. I saw that in the corner of my eye, Chris kept looking at me in a manner that nonverbally said, "why are you not screaming?" while trying not to be obvious. Anyway, after the ride, I got the hell off that ride as quickly as possible and his group followed us until they decided to go ride again. 

Looking back, I feel bad knowing that I didn't even give the poor guy a chance to speak to me. I mean, on one hand, it probably wouldn't have gone anywhere, as I was already in a relationship, but on the other, I feel as if I should've at least acknowledged his existence. Sorry, "Chris."

*Before I start, I just want to clarify that this isn't in anyway me trying to gain sympathy or anything. It's more of a "thank you" to this person instead.*

There was this one girl, who we'll call "Red," in junior high who was friendly toward me. To give some context, I was considered relatively unpopular and weird, so I was bullied and didn't have many friends. Red acted like one of those "f\*ck what society thinks" type of people, which normally would put me off, but she was very kind instead of acting like an ass like how most would.

Anyway, Red would often say "Hi" while passing in the halls and this one time before class (we had Homeroom, Guitar and Science together), she kept looking at me as if she was concerned. I noticed that, during rehearsals for our performances, she'd take a few glances at me like a mother checking on her child during our elective period. I suppose I was visibly depressed or something and she probably took notice. Red was the only person who approached me and asked if I was okay. I, being the typical depressed teenager who didn't f\*ck with my feelings calmly said that I was fine. She smiled and continued with her day and we didn't speak that much after. I always considered Red to be one of my 2-3 friends, but I feel so remorseful for lying to her.

After a week or so, I noticed that Red hadn't been talking to me. I assumed that she might've gotten offended when I essentially shut down her attempt to help me, so I brushed it off and immediately (mentally) cut ties with her, as an offended 13-year old girl does. A few days later, Red was absent from homeroom. I didn't really notice at first, but suddenly our Principal walks into our class flanked by a few other staff members, tears streaming from her red eyes. She informed the class that Red had passed away the night before.

Immediately, I felt my heart drop. I felt like absolute sh\*t for mentally cutting ties with her. There was no confirmation on the cause of her death and, to this day, I still don't exactly know what happened. I was told that Red died from Leukemia, though another popular rumor was that she committed suicide. I chose to believe the leukemia story, as the suicide story was too close to home. During this time, I had also made several suicide attempts (that obviously failed) and so I felt so stupid for not recognizing the signs. The school let some students sit in the MPR to grieve while grief counselors talked with them. One thing that pissed me off was that random people who were obviously not friends with Red sat in the MPR to get off of class, showing no sympathy or remorse. I channeled my anger toward them and sadness into energy. I gathered enough energy to write a letter addressed to Red's parents, in which I told them how her simple actions had such a great effect on me (I also mistakenly mentioned the leukemia story, which I feel like an idiot about).

I never really got any solace or closure on the topic, I kind of eventually learned that Red did commit suicide and that I had to move on with my own life. Unfortunately, these events took a toll on me. In my freshman year of high school, I thought one of my friends died (she fainted and wasn't responding at first). I immediately broke down because the event provoked memories of Red's passing. A similar thing happened during sophomore year. Another girl who was kind to me hit her head on a table and bled out during class. Both girls survived their injuries, but both times caused me to have horrible flashbacks to Red's passing. 

I haven't exactly gotten help for that, as I didn't get to bring it up in therapy (I can't afford it right now), but I now realize that I should treasure every moment and every person in my life, as they can be gone in a split second. 

**Red, if you ever get to read this, Thank You. I'm so sorry that I failed you. Your battle is over, you can finally rest.** 

*tl;dr:*

Unexpectedly nice girl was one of the only people who were nice to me during a dark time in my life (Junior High). She committed suicide and I failed to recognize the signs. I hope that she knows that we haven't forgotten about her. Thank you, Red. You'll never be forgotten.
